revisions.before:
This formulation delivers a major operational advantage over naive company-by-company confidence intervals: **Exact Cancellation of Shared-Source Errors**. If two companies evaluated by the same linear model share an identical additive error from a common industry benchmark or third-party sensor feed, then $`B_i = B_k`$ along those coordinates and:

$$
a_f = (B_i - B_k)^\top \beta_f = 0 \implies h_U(\pm a_f) = 0
$$

The common error cancels identically in the pairwise comparison!
revisions.after:
This formulation delivers a major operational advantage over naive company-by-company confidence intervals: **Exact Cancellation of Shared-Source Errors**. Let $`S`$ index shared-source coordinates on which the two companies have identical loadings, so $`(B_i-B_k)_{:,S}=0`$. Under the same linear scoring model:

$$
(a_f)_S=0,\qquad \Delta_f(u)=m_f+(a_f)_{S^c}^{\top}u_{S^c}
$$

The shared-source contribution cancels identically in the pairwise comparison; company-specific uncertainty remains in the support-function bound. If all uncertain directions cancel, then $`a_f=0`$ and $`h_U(\pm a_f)=0`$.
revisions.reason: Equality only on shared columns kills only the corresponding components of a_f, not all company-specific components. Counterexample loadings Bi=(1,1), Bk=(1,0), beta=1 leaves a=(0,1).
sourceRefs: Project 4: mathematical definition and derivation cited in the revision reason

revisions.before: When frontier AI labs partnered with research universities in autumn 2023 to probe the limits of scientific reasoning, the standard playbook was simple: collect difficult STEM problems and check whether the model's final answer matched the answer key. Our experiments quickly revealed why this approach hit a dead end: models frequently arrived at the right number via broken physical assumptions, brute-force computational exhaustion, or unauthorized tool calls (such as invoking a Python VM in a compliance-restricted workflow that mandated Excel). Sections I–VII below present the formal mathematical and engineering architecture I developed in 2023 to turn scientific benchmarking into a rigorous, certificate-backed supervision system.
revisions.after: The collaboration began in autumn 2023 with scientific-reasoning tasks for frontier models. Initial experiments in our workflow showed why final-answer matching was insufficient: a correct number could coexist with an invalid physical assumption, an unsupported computational shortcut, or a tool call that violated the task’s specified execution policy. Sections I–VII formalize the resulting acceptance architecture and relate it to subsequent process-evaluation research; the project start date does not imply that every later citation or mathematical formulation was part of the initial workflow.
revisions.reason: Avoids a universal claim about the standard playbook at all AI labs and separates the original task work from later formalization.

Designed evidence-tracing and verification controls for private-market and ESG research, where report-level review alone may leave shared-source errors and unresolved factual claims undetected.
revisions.reason: Preserves the concrete engineering problem and controls while removing unsupported prevalence, intent, solved-problem, and regulatory-vacuum assertions.

revisions.before: When global alternative asset managers evaluate private equity and impact investments, ESG and operational risk diligence cannot rely on naive LLM summarization. Between 2023 and 2026, we observed a structural shift in corporate self-reporting: just as local merchants learned to manipulate AI recommendation engines via coordinated digital marketing, corporate issuers began deploying AI-optimized sustainability narratives to inflate automated ESG scores. Because regulatory legislation and enforcement mechanisms have not yet caught up with AI-driven narrative manipulation, an investment workflow that takes unverified corporate disclosures at face value—or ranks diligence priorities solely by raw SHAP values—exposes the fund to severe greenwashing risk. Sections I–VI below present the mathematical and systems architecture I developed to audit score credibility, cancel shared measurement errors, and route human diligence toward the exact claims that govern the investment decision.
revisions.after: In private-equity and impact-investment diligence, fluent summaries do not establish the truth of corporate disclosures. The workflow treats AI-polished narratives, unsupported sustainability claims, and shared reporting errors as risks to the credibility of automated ESG and investment scores. Existing disclosure and antifraud obligations do not remove the analyst’s need to verify material evidence. Sections I–VI present the mathematical and systems architecture I developed to audit score credibility, account for shared measurement errors, and route human diligence toward claims capable of changing the comparison.
revisions.reason: The SEC has taken ESG and AI-marketing enforcement actions. They refute a broad vacuum claim but do not establish that every AI-generated narrative tactic is covered or effectively detected.

revisions.before: In high-compliance financial and academic environments, spinning up an arbitrary Python virtual machine introduces severe security and audit risks, requiring tasks to be solved strictly within approved, auditable toolkits (such as Excel).
revisions.after: When a task’s specified data-governance policy permits only the approved Excel environment, an unauthorized Python virtual machine violates that execution policy.
revisions.reason: Tool compliance depends on the specified organizational task policy; there is no general financial or academic rule that forbids Python or mandates Excel.
